title: Space Force Pays Rocket Lab $397 Million for 'Flatellites' to Track Threats
summary:
In a major boost to national defense, Rocket Lab has secured a $397 million contract from the U.S. Space Force to design, manufacture, and launch a fleet of 'Flatellites'—flat satellites optimized for tracking airborne threats in real time. The project is part of the Space Force's Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program, which aims to enhance the military's ability to monitor contested airspace.

The flat design is a key innovation: it allows more satellites to be packed into a single launch, making it ideal for large orbital constellations. The satellites will be equipped with low-latency, high-bandwidth communication systems and advanced sensors to detect adversarial aircraft and missiles.

Rocket Lab CEO Peter Beck expressed pride in contributing to 'a resilient space-based sensing layer' that will strengthen the Joint Force's capabilities. This contract is the company's largest national defense deal this year, and it's part of a broader surge in defense spending on space technology.

Since January 2026, Rocket Lab has announced four major government contracts totaling $943 million, including $190 million for hypersonic test launches, $90 million for two geostationary satellites, and $266 million for missile-defense missions from Alaska. The company also unveiled GHOST, a deployable shipping-container-based launch system that can support responsive missions from mobile locations.

'We've mastered the art of building launch sites. Now we're making them deployable worldwide,' Beck said during a recent earnings call.

The Flatellites will launch in stacks aboard Rocket Lab's upcoming Neutron rocket, which is designed to compete with SpaceX's Falcon 9 in lift capability and partial reusability. Neutron is expected to debut later this year or in early 2027.

This contract underscores the growing importance of space-based defense systems, especially amid plans for a 'Golden Dome' missile-defense shield in orbit. Rocket Lab's innovative approach could set a new standard for how we build and deploy satellites for national security.
why_it_matters: This story shows how private companies and the military are merging in space, which could speed up new technology but also raises big questions about security, debris, and who controls orbit. The satellites being built now may be part of the defense and communications systems you grow up with.

background_read: The U.S. Space Force is the military service responsible for organizing, training, and equipping forces to protect American interests in space; it has become a major customer for private launch companies.
Rocket Lab, founded by Peter Beck and headquartered in the United States and New Zealand, began with small Electron rockets and has grown into satellite manufacturing and larger launch vehicles.
SpaceX's Falcon 9, mentioned as the rocket Neutron will compete with, is a partially reusable launch vehicle that has dramatically lowered the cost of sending payloads to orbit.

The 'Golden Dome' is a proposed space-based missile-defense shield that would use sensors and interceptors in orbit to detect and stop missile threats; such programs have renewed attention on space-based sensing.

Moving-target indicator systems, originally developed for aircraft radar, allow operators to see moving objects against a cluttered background—moving that capability to orbit could expand coverage far beyond traditional airspace.

perspectives.description: Space Force and defense planners see Flatellites as a way to gain faster, more resilient surveillance of moving threats. Rocket Lab's flat-pack design could make large constellations cheaper and quicker to deploy.
Critics worry that an orbital arms race could make space more dangerous and crowded. More military satellites may increase the risk of collisions, debris, and miscalculation between rival powers.

From a systems view, this contract reflects a broader shift from traditional government-run space programs to commercial companies providing defense services. It also shows how design choices—like flattening a satellite—can change launch economics and military strategy.

If Neutron succeeds, reusable rockets may become a major part of military launches, lowering costs and enabling rapid replacement of damaged satellites. The next few years will show whether this model makes space defense more resilient or more contested.
